idiom_name: sqlx Transaction (begin/commit, rollback on drop) + hand-written change set
implementation_notes: Rust's ecosystem provides the boundary with a safety net and nothing else: sqlx's Pool::begin or Connection::begin returns a Transaction that dereferences to the connection, must end in commit() or rollback(), and calls rollback on drop if neither happened, so a forgotten commit is a silent rollback rather than a partial write. There is no identity map and no dirty tracking in std, so the register half is yours: keep a change set (new, dirty, removed) keyed by id and flush it inside the transaction. Diesel offers the same boundary as a closure (conn.transaction(|conn| ...)) and uses savepoints when nested; SeaORM adds ActiveModel with Set(...)/save() plus a closure or begin/commit transaction, but still writes eagerly per model rather than deferring a flush.
pitfalls: Borrow rules bite here: the change set must not borrow the connection while the transaction is open - own the data or split the phases.
A missing commit() rolls back silently, which looks like a successful write that changed nothing.
A Transaction borrows the connection mutably, so helpers must take &mut *tx (or &mut **tx for executors); holding two references is a compile error, not a runtime bug.
SeaORM's save() writes immediately - wrapping it in a transaction makes the writes atomic but not batched into one round trip.

variants.name: SeaORM ActiveModel save() inside a transaction
variants.implementation_notes: SeaORM models the writable side with ActiveModel: Set(...) marks changed fields, save(txn) emits the INSERT or UPDATE immediately, and db.transaction(|txn| ...) or begin/commit wraps the sequence atomically (nested transactions use SAVEPOINT). It is the closest Rust gets to a framework-provided unit of work without deferred flush: the transaction is the unit of work and ActiveModel is the per-row mapper, but nothing collects changes for you.
pitfalls: The async closure must be pinned (Box::pin) because async closures are not stable; capturing references across it is the usual source of lifetime errors.
Dropping the transaction without commit rolls back, so an early return path can discard work that looked finished.

variants.name: Diesel Connection::transaction closure (sync, savepoint-aware)
variants.implementation_notes: Diesel exposes the unit of work as a closure on the connection: the block runs inside a transaction, commits when it returns Ok and rolls back on Err, and a nested transaction on the same connection becomes a savepoint instead of a second transaction. Error::RollbackTransaction forces a rollback without inventing an error, and the change set is whatever the closure executes, so tracking stays in application code.
pitfalls: The closure receives the connection mutably, so the change set cannot hold it - collect ids/values before the call.
A failed commit triggers an attempted rollback; if that also fails the connection is marked broken and all further transaction work on it errors.
